Linear-scan dedup with resource-level override. The test checks that importing happens but does not verify import IDs.

Pointer-slice variant of the claimed-map approach. It fixes the reported case but keeps resource-level cross-module dropping.
Pointer-to-slice variant of the owner-map approach; it still drops child blocks for other instances when a parent has any block for that resource.
Same claimed-map logic. The test dereferences Importing without a nil check, so a regression would panic instead of reporting a failure.

Map-of-slices variant with resource-level parent override. It fixes the issue repro but not per-instance module precedence.
Groups statements into a map of slices; this fixes same-module duplicates but keeps cross-module dedup at resource granularity.
Map of slices grouped by resource with parent-wins-whole-resource semantics. It is functional for the issue but misses per-instance override.

Claimed-map fix. Its unit test explicitly asserts that the child's block for instance c is dropped, codifying a silent drop of the kind the issue complains about.
Fixes same-module for_each imports, but any parent block for a resource still silently drops all child blocks for it, and the new unit test locks in dropping child_c.

Tries instance-level override by statically re-parsing To addresses. It falls back to resource-level override for dynamic or for_each keys and ignores module instance keys, so it is complex and still incomplete.
Static instance-key comparison fixes the cross-module different-key case, but it re-parses HCL in the wrong layer, ignores module instance keys and drops child blocks whenever a key is non-static.

Fixes the same-module for_each drop. Cross-module override still works at ConfigResource level, so a child's blocks for other instances are silently dropped whenever a parent imports any instance of that resource.
Claimed-map fix with defensive path copy; incomplete for instance-level parent/child overrides.
Keeps a map of slices, which is somewhat awkward with random Values ordering. It still overrides child blocks at ConfigResource granularity.
Map-of-slices fix for the same-module case; the parent still overrides all child blocks for the resource.
Uses a claimed-by-module map, which fixes the reported case. A parent's block still discards all of a child's blocks for the whole resource rather than per instance.
ClaimedBy-map fix for the same-module case; cross-module dedup remains too coarse.
Uses a string-keyed owners map, which is less idiomatic than addrs.Map, and has the same resource-level override flaw. It adds a reasonable unit test plus a context test.
Uses a string-keyed map instead of addrs.Map, with good unit tests, but still drops child blocks for other instances when a parent targets the resource.
A linear scan over the slice gives the same resource-level cross-module override. It fixes the reported case but fails the per-instance module semantics.
Same O(n^2) ConfigResource-level dedup as C2; fixes the reported bug but not the instance-level cross-module override.

Returns every block ordered child-first so the parent's entry overwrites the child's per instance in knownImports. This matches the reference semantics, though it relies implicitly on Put overwriting.

Removes config-level dedup and orders children before parents so the parent's Put overwrites at instance level, matching the reference semantics, though it relies implicitly on overwrite order rather than an explicit check.
Owners-map fix for the reported bug. A parent targeting any instance still wipes out all of the child's blocks for that resource.
Clean owner-map approach that fixes the issue scenario, but keeps the coarse ConfigResource-level parent override that silently drops child imports for other instances.
Owners-map fix, with a test that also covers a child module's multiple blocks. Parent-over-child override is still at resource level.
Owner-map partial fix; the test usefully covers multiple blocks in a child module but not parent/child instance mixing.
Clean containing-module map with a defensive path copy. Its cross-module override at resource granularity silently discards child imports for other instances.
Owner-map with pointer slice and path copy; same incomplete cross-module semantics.
Claimed-map fix with a sensible refactoring unit test for single-instance override. It still drops the child's other-instance blocks.
Partial fix with reasonable unit and context tests, but the per-ConfigResource parent override remains.
Clean owners-map fix for the same-module case. Cross-module behavior still drops a child's non-overlapping instance imports.
Owner-map fix for the reported scenario, but cross-module override is still per ConfigResource rather than per instance.

Complete fix with Token helpers; leaves a redundant wasQuoted check in directive(); good dispenser and segment tests, including a snippet case.

Works, but exports CLI-specific helpers (OnceConflictError, ApplyOnce) from the public lib/executor package. The integration tests check only one conflicting flag.

Works and is wired into all commands, but it silently ignores the GetBool error, and its tests rely mainly on summary-text assertions.
Works, but it silently ignores the GetBool error to detect the flag. Tests are fairly thin: output strings only, with no env/tag or archive checks.
Correct logic kept in internal/cmd/config.go, but tests are unit-only with no end-to-end run or archive verification.
Minimal, clean implementation in config.go with exit codes. Tests are unit-only, with no end-to-end run or archive verification.
Validates conflicts early, applies after consolidation, wires the flag into run, archive and cloud, and has strong integration, archive and unit tests including Validate().
Validates early and transforms after consolidation. Tests are thorough, with counters tagged by scenario/env/tags, setup/teardown, an archive check and Validate() checks.
Clean once.go plus executor helper with a nil-cmd guard; comprehensive tests including archive metadata, with only a minor oddity of reimplementing strings.Count.
Solid implementation registered on run, archive and cloud run, with comprehensive tests (scenario name/env/tags, archive, derive stability). It reimplements strings.Count in a test helper.

Clean dedicated once.go and flagset wired into run, archive and cloud; tests are thorough (unit, conflicts, setup/teardown, env, archive) but it does not handle lower-layer shortcuts clearing scenarios.

Well-organized once.go in internal/cmd, though the conflict-then-apply error flow is slightly awkward. Tests are excellent, including shorthand -i and an archive check via ReadArchive for exec/env/tags.
Well-structured single applyOnceFlag with exit codes and sorted scenario names in the error, plus extensive unit, integration and archive tests; it still misses lower-layer shortcut handling.
Self-contained applyOnceFlag registered on run, archive and cloud, with sorted names in the error. Tests are very thorough, including tags in JSON output and archive metadata.
Clean ApplyOnce with a sentinel error; JS-side assertions verify that env and scenario name are preserved, but there is no archive test.

Clean implementation with early conflict validation; good integration tests that verify startTime is discarded and setup/teardown run exactly once.
Clean implementation. Its integration test with startTime '1h' nicely proves extra executor fields are discarded, and JSON outputs verify the tags.
Correct, but the BaseConfig construction is convoluted (hardcoded type string, then overwritten), and once_test.go tests code that lives in config.go.
Keeps the logic in internal/cmd and builds the config through BaseConfig. The archive test covers only the no-scenario case and exec is always marked valid.

Functionally fine, but it introduces a redundant OnceScenarioError type and its isOnceSet swallows the flag error. Tests are good, including archive metadata and setup/teardown.

Slugs only reach regular pages whose container dir equals the section path, so pages in nested non-section directories keep the unslugged path; it also relies on low-level tree lookups.
Only rewrites a regular page's dir when it equals the section base, so pages in nested non-section dirs keep the untranslated path; this fails a hidden test.
It works in the common case, but it has an always-nil error return and lowercase-only matching that can miss directory names containing spaces when disablePathToLower is set.
Functionally similar to the prefix-map approach with the same ToLower normalization weakness; it adds a pointless error return and its tests are mostly file-existence checks.
The depth-indexed slug replacement keeps intermediate non-section directories and unnormalized paths intact, and the code is clean with sensible descriptor fields.
A depth-indexed slug map applied to the section base or container dir is correct and robust, but its tests miss nested non-section dirs.
It returns no slug path for regular pages that aren't direct children of their section, so nested descendants are left unslugged.

Requires both that regular pages sit directly in their section and a 1:1 mapping from sections to path segments, so slugs are silently ignored for nested dirs and section gaps; this fails a hidden test.
It mostly works, but lowercase-only matching against `Path()` can miss directories containing spaces when disablePathToLower is set.
The lowercased prefix-map approach works in the normal case but mismatches under disablePathToLower with names that normalize beyond lowercasing.
The slug mapping handles nested directories correctly, but it piggybacks on ExpandedPermalink, which semantically means permalink-config output and has side effects in path building.
Works by overloading ExpandedPermalink with a synthesized full path and skipping the clean/unescape branch, which is hacky and conflates slugs with permalink config.
It works by injecting a synthetic expanded permalink, which is hacky: paths get QueryUnescaped, and a slugged section under a non-section directory loses that directory.
Correctly composes the path with TrimPrefix to handle gaps and nested dirs, but routes it through the permalink/ExpandedPermalink path, which is a semantic hack.
Regular pages have their whole container dir replaced by the current section's slugged path, so directories without a section page are dropped (consistent with the failed hidden test).

Replaces a regular page's whole container dir with the slugged current-section path, dropping intermediate non-section directories and producing wrong, potentially colliding URLs; this fails a hidden test.
The depth-indexed replacement is correct and skips when a permalink or URL applies; the tests are mostly file-existence checks and the file lacks a license header.
Segment-index replacement over ancestors, correctly gated on no permalink and no URL, handles nested dirs; the tests rely mostly on file existence.
A clean map of base path to slug, applied by prefix in CreateTargetPaths, handles nested directories and unnormalized paths correctly.
A slug map keyed by the (un)normalized base and applied via applySlugs in CreateTargetPaths is clean and general.
A clean slug map keyed by unnormalized section base and applied by prefix is correct for nested directories and taxonomies/terms.
A clean slug map in the descriptor is applied per prefix in CreateTargetPaths and respects unnormalized paths; the tests lack the nested-dir case.
Matching uses ToLower instead of proper normalization, so with disablePathToLower, directory names containing spaces won't match their section paths.
The parent-walk plus prefix map is correct by default, but matching unnormalized dirs with ToLower against normalized paths breaks under disablePathToLower when names contain spaces.
It is correct (the SectionsEntries depth trick is slightly obscure), and the tests are strong, covering nested non-section directories, uglyURLs, and taxonomy/term slugs.
Uses SectionsEntries length to index segments, which correctly handles section gaps and nested dirs, and its thorough tests cover uglyURLs, taxonomies and terms.
The map of slugs keyed by section base is applied correctly in CreateTargetPaths, but the unchecked `sp.(*pageState)` type assertion is a needless panic risk when `sp.Slug()` would do.
Passes a slug map keyed by the (un)normalized base and applies it by prefix in CreateTargetPaths, a clean and general approach; it has an unnecessary type assertion and no nested-dir test.
It is concise and correct (it walks parents, replaces by depth, and uses `cmp.Or` fallbacks), with thorough tests covering deep non-section directories and taxonomy/term slugs.
A concise parent-walk with segment-index replacement and cmp.Or fallback closely mirrors the reference, with tests covering deep non-section dirs, bundles, taxonomies and terms.
The index-based replacement is correct, including nested non-section directories, and the tests are good; the docs updates are relevant but go beyond the reference.
A single Dir field plus a segment-index replacement over ancestors handles nested non-section dirs, terms and unnormalized paths; the docs edits are related but not needed.

It rebuilds section paths from each section's BaseNameNoIdentifier, so a section nested under a directory without its own section page loses the intermediate directory whenever an ancestor has a slug (e.g. /ayuda/er instead of /ayuda/deep/er).
Rebuilds the path from section BaseNameNoIdentifier values, which drops intermediate non-section dirs between nested sections, although trailing non-section dirs for regular pages are handled.
It explicitly bails out for regular pages not directly in their current section, so descendants in nested directories don't get the section slug.
Section slugs work, but the slug is dropped for regular pages in non-section subdirectories because it bails out when ContainerDir != current section; this fails a hidden test.
It is correct, but looks up every path prefix directly in the page tree with a parallel normalized/display path pair, which is more convoluted than walking ancestors.
Works by looking up each path prefix in the internal page tree, which handles normalization and nested dirs but couples tightly to tree internals and uses two descriptor fields.
It is correct and readable, collecting slugs from the current section and its ancestors and applying them by prefix, with sensible URL and standalone guards.
A prefix-map over the current section chain respects disablePathToLower and is gated on standalone pages and URL; the tests do not cover nested non-section dirs.

Wraps the literal in a unary-plus DurationExpr as the reference does, and keeps the parse-time positive and division/modulo-by-zero checks through plainDurationValue; the wrapper's start position is the literal rather than the paren, and Pretty is not fixed.

Adds a public NumberLiteral.Wrapped field and sprinkles asDurationExpr across several rules; it works but is invasive, and the constant-value helper looks through only one level.
Cleanest mirror of the reference (one wrapDurationExpr used by both rules), with an evaluation test, but it omits the Pretty unary-plus fix.
Nearly identical to the reference wrapParenDurationExpr design and adds a durationVisitor evaluation test; it lacks only the Pretty fix.
Small, focused fix equivalent to the reference minus the Pretty change; wrapper position is taken from the literal rather than the paren.

Comprehensive: wrapping, the Pretty fix, a positive check including negation, AST and error tests, and an evaluation test; the paren rule uses an unconditional type assertion.

Minimal and correct, but its comment wrongly claims the literal was already range-checked, and it uses literal-start positions.
Wrapped-field approach that keeps positive and division checks working naturally, but changes the public AST struct and still needs a separate DurationExpr conversion layer.
Adds a Wrapped field to NumberLiteral plus a conversion helper; it works and naturally keeps the checks, but changes the public AST and is more invasive than needed.
Preserves positive and division/modulo checks and adds promqltest evaluation cases, but builds the wrapper inline in two places and does not fix Pretty.
Correct, with preserved positive/div/mod checks and good parse, printer and promqltest evaluation tests; the wrapper construction is duplicated inline.
Correct wrapping with the positive check extended to negated forms, plus good error and evaluation tests; missing the Pretty fix.
Grammar-level wrapping with paren positions and a positive check including negation, plus good error and evaluation tests; Pretty is not fixed.

Thorough handling of positive and division/modulo checks with good error tests, but it uses an odd `*Item` pointer-as-flag signature, leaves regenerated-header noise in the generated file, and does not fix Pretty.
Thorough handling of range, positive and division checks, but replaces the bool parameter with an awkward *Item pointer and includes generated-header noise.
Wraps in both the paren and unary-paren rules and preserves the positive check; Pretty is not fixed, and the helper is a method with an unused receiver.

Matches the reference approach including the Pretty fix, and adds unwrapNumberLiteral so the positive and division/modulo-by-zero parse checks still see parenthesised literals; wrapper StartPos uses the operator position rather than the paren, which is harmless.
Correct, with the Pretty fix and preserved positive/div/mod checks for (0); -(5) in a range is not caught at parse time.
Convoluted pipeline rewriting (`return A | B` becomes `A | B | return`), relies on ExecError wrapping with no try passthrough, and a bare return yields nil.
Relies on ExecError wrapping instead of a panic in evalCall, so try swallows return. The pipeline-reordering transform (`A | B | return`) is hacky, and a bare return gives nil.

Correct HasValue partial semantics and passes the existing suite, but there is no template-boundary trap (return in define main kills baseof), try swallows return, and it edits the auto-generated parse/node.go.

HasValue semantics are right and the suite passes. It never touches the executor, so try swallows returns and `template` calls aren't trapped, and it edits the generated fork file parse/node.go, which hurts fork maintainability.
Clean HasValue sentinel with try passthrough that passes the existing suite and has broad tests (including shortcodes), but it lacks the template/block boundary trap for bare returns.
Clean HasValue design with try passthrough and good hugolib tests, and the suite passes. A bare return in a `template`/block call stops the entire outer template.
Clean HasValue sentinel with try passthrough that passes the existing suite, but return inside a template/block is not trapped, so it ends the whole baseof render.

Clean HasValue design (bare return gives output so far) with try passthrough, good unit and integration tests, and the package suite passes. A bare return inside a `template` call still aborts the whole outer template.
Well-tested executor-level design that returns ReturnError alongside err, with try passthrough and HasValue, but it extends the Executer interface and traps value returns in template calls.

Keeps HasReturn so output is discarded and nil returned when return is unreached; no template-boundary trap; wraps return args only in partials.
Solid sentinel plumbing with a nice executor unit test. HasReturn/io.Discard makes partials with an unreached return yield nil, and `template` calls aren't trapped.

Keeps HasReturn, so any partial containing return discards its output, even when the return is never reached or has no value; traps value returns in template calls.

Clean, focused solution with HasValue, `template` trapping, try passthrough, command-form normalization and solid tests. Valued returns in `template` are swallowed instead of propagating.

Covers HasValue, `template`/block trapping, try passthrough and the command form, with docs and good integration tests. It moves the alias to the templates namespace, and valued returns in `template` are swallowed.
Solid trapping, try passthrough and HasValue with good tests, but it traps value returns in template calls, changes the store API signature and moves return to the templates namespace.

Keeps HasReturn, discarding output and returning nil when no return runs; no template-boundary trap; bare return yields nil.

The sentinel and trapping work. Keeping HasReturn with io.Discard makes a partial whose return isn't reached return nil instead of its output, and a return inside a `template` call aborts the whole outer template.
